Like most mathematicians, I believed the Riemann Hypothesis to be completely out of reach at present (even with the best AI tools), because I expected it to require substantial theory-building, probably in arithmetic geometry. The kind of new theory-building that fills entire books, and that AI isn't so good at yet.

Mathematicians have a notion of how deep a problem is. A sufficiently deep problem is generally intractable until enough of the theory is in place. If difficult problems are like valuable mineral reserves buried miles underground, you first need to build the infrastructure to reach them.

What Levent's proof seems to have done instead is something completely different. It takes an incredibly complicated tour through the infrastructure built for a hundred other mineral reserves, situated far from the destination, and somehow create a wormhole to the original destination.

This is not theory-building in the usual sense. It is something much weirder and more alien. The best human mathematicians know how to build theory, painstakingly, to reach a goal. But no human brain, on its own, is capable of creating a wormhole that requires a 25,000 page long tour through existing infrastructure with no obvious or realistic connection to the goal. But huge credit to Levent here: I think no current AI, on its own, is capable of this either.

I had never worked on or thought too much about the Riemann Hypothesis: it seemed very far removed from my own area of number theory.

But the astonishing thing about Levent's claimed proof of RH (which I think has a very good chance of being correct) is that it uses a huge number of precisely the things that are central to my own corner of number theory:

- Theta functions and other automorphic forms on unitary groups
- Gan–Gross–Prasad period formulas
- Relative trace formulas

Etc., etc.

A problem that I had always assumed would require new theories in arithmetic geometry may instead turn out to be tractable through an inhuman chain of existing (deep) results in higher-rank automorphic forms (and a lot else).

My weekend thoughts on #uranium, #silver, #gold and HydroGraph $HGRAF

Uranium stocks have been hammered. Uranium itself is still around $90/lb. I expect a much higher uranium price in 2027, and I’m still waiting another month or two before adding heavily to the miners. Here’s why.

Uranium

When uranium juniors sell off across the board, I look at how much drilling each one can fund with the cash it already has. The drill program costs just as much after a sell-off. If the share price halves, an explorer has to issue twice as many shares to raise the same money. And that assumes investors are willing to write the cheque.

Producers have their own problem. Miss a production target and you may have to buy uranium on the spot market to deliver into a contract you signed years ago at a lower price. Meanwhile, the cost of labour, materials and construction has gone up. How sad is that? You are a producer, the LT price is ok, but you keep losing money because of past mistakes.

Look at what the big producers actually got paid in Q3. Spot averaged US$88.56/lb. Kazatomprom’s group realized US$81.50. Cameco realized US$65.78. That’s nearly US$23 below spot for Cameco. My view is that producers locked in too many pounds too cheaply. Utilities will have to offer better terms if they want someone to build the next generation of mines.

And does $90/lb really sound expensive? Uranium hit $136 in 2007. That was nearly 20 years of inflation ago. At today’s construction costs, plenty of greenfield projects still struggle to offer a return worth the risk. Even at $150/lb, I’d question how quickly the industry could deliver enough uranium. A utility can raise its bid tomorrow. A miner still needs years to permit, finance and build.

I expect larger producers to pick up some of the better juniors. Others could face another round of selling if their market caps fall far enough to get them dropped from an index. I’m looking for cash in the bank, a manageable burn rate and projects whose economics hold up at today’s costs. For investors who want exposure to physical uranium, there’s #SPUT. For a basket of miners, there are uranium equity ETFs.

One more thing to remember when the tide turns. If the juniors double or triple, expect a wave of financings. A CEO who struggled to raise money at the bottom will take that call at twice the price.

Gold, silver and the signal I’m watching

With uranium, I can look at what utilities need and what the mines can deliver. Gold and silver are harder to call. Investment flows can turn quickly, and silver has industrial demand in the mix as well.

Right now, I’m watching oil. A sustained drop should feed through to lower headline inflation over the coming months. If markets start pricing in rate cuts and real yields roll over, I expect gold and silver to turn well before the first cut. Easier financing would give uranium equities room to run, too. Until then, I see more downside in precious metals.

Why HydroGraph is my largest holding

How do you sell serious tonnage of a material that works at a dose of just 200 grams? Look at what those 200 grams go into.

In a peer-reviewed study published in October, Arizona State researchers used 200 grams of HydroGraph graphene per tonne of binder in 3D-printed mortar. They measured gains of up to 25% in compressive and flexural strength. At that dose, every million tonnes of binder treated would use 200 tonnes of graphene. That’s why the size of the end market matters so much to me.

The plastics results are just as striking. In HydroGraph’s epoxy tests, replacing a small amount of carbon black with 0.04% graphene cut electrical resistivity to one-110th of its original value. The total amount of conductive filler stayed the same.

My favourite example comes from DB Chem. It needed an antistatic plastic film, but even at 30% carbon black, the affordable grade couldn’t meet the target. With 15% carbon black and just 0.2% HydroGraph graphene, the film hit the target, was easier to form and cost about the same to formulate. That’s a result a purchasing manager can act on.

Then there’s Sparc Technologies. After 16 weeks of corrosion testing, rust had spread 25% less from a scratch in a commercial epoxy coating containing Sparc’s HydroGraph-based additive. Sparc says a successful 4,200-hour test would take the companies into negotiations for a supply agreement. That’s one potential customer with a specific result and a clear next decision.

CEO Kjirstin Breure’s two November interviews with Jay Taylor are worth putting together. On November 5, she explained how the graphene paste makes it easier for manufacturers to use the material. More than 30 customers have already received samples. In the November 19 follow-up, she discussed patents for specific applications, including conductive plastics, and said a manufacturer was already lined up to build more Hyperion reactors.

Several customers have moved on to negotiating prices, volumes and supply terms. And look at who HydroGraph hired this week to close those deals. New chief commercial officer Hector Miravete previously led commercial strategy for a Johnson Matthey catalyst portfolio generating more than $700 million in annual revenue. He knows what it takes to sell a specialized material to industrial buyers year after year.

Now put the capital requirements alongside the mining economics above. HydroGraph raised C$70.4 million. What does it cost to get Bellville up and running? Roughly US$8 million for the building and its first six reactors, according to CEO Kjirstin Breure. That gives HydroGraph about 60 tons of annual capacity at Bellville, with room to scale to 360 as orders come in.

I expect hockey-stick revenue growth to begin in 2027, and I see a credible path to break-even that year without another equity raise. The milestone I’m watching most closely is the first repeat order with meaningful volume. That’s when we start to learn what one qualified application is worth to HydroGraph every year. Then run the same exercise across plastics, coatings, cement and rubber. That’s why $HGRAF is my number one investment.

Just my weekend thoughts. As always, do your own DD.

If the share price halves, an explorer has to issue twice as many shares to raise the same money. And that assumes investors are willing to write the cheque.

Producers have their own problem. Miss a production target and you may have to buy uranium on the spot market to deliver into a contract you signed years ago at a lower price. Meanwhile, the cost of labour, materials and construction has gone up. How sad is that? You are a producer, the LT price is ok, but you keep losing money because of past mistakes.

Look at what the big producers actually got paid in Q3. Spot averaged US$88.56/lb. Kazatomprom’s group realized US$81.50. Cameco realized US$65.78. That’s nearly US$23 below spot for Cameco. My view is that producers locked in too many pounds too cheaply. Utilities will have to offer better terms if they want someone to build the next generation of mines.

And does $90/lb really sound expensive? Uranium hit $136 in 2007. That was nearly 20 years of inflation ago. At today’s construction costs, plenty of greenfield projects still struggle to offer a return worth the risk. Even at $150/lb, I’d question how quickly the industry could deliver enough uranium. A utility can raise its bid tomorrow. A miner still needs years to permit, finance and build.

I expect larger producers to pick up some of the better juniors. Others could face another round of selling if their market caps fall far enough to get them dropped from an index. I’m looking for cash in the bank, a manageable burn rate and projects whose economics hold up at today’s costs. For investors who want exposure to physical uranium, there’s #SPUT. For a basket of miners, there are uranium equity ETFs.

One more thing to remember when the tide turns. If the juniors double or triple, expect a wave of financings. A CEO who struggled to raise money at the bottom will take that call at twice the price.

Gold, silver and the signal I’m watching

With uranium, I can look at what utilities need and what the mines can deliver. Gold and silver are harder to call. Investment flows can turn quickly, and silver has industrial demand in the mix as well.

Right now, I’m watching oil. A sustained drop should feed through to lower headline inflation over the coming months. If markets start pricing in rate cuts and real yields roll over, I expect gold and silver to turn well before the first cut. Easier financing would give uranium equities room to run, too. Until then, I see more downside in precious metals.

Why HydroGraph is my largest holding

How do you sell serious tonnage of a material that works at a dose of just 200 grams? Look at what those 200 grams go into.

In a peer-reviewed study published in October, Arizona State researchers used 200 grams of HydroGraph graphene per tonne of binder in 3D-printed mortar. They measured gains of up to 25% in compressive and flexural strength. At that dose, every million tonnes of binder treated would use 200 tonnes of graphene. That’s why the size of the end market matters so much to me.

The plastics results are just as striking. In HydroGraph’s epoxy tests, replacing a small amount of carbon black with 0.04% graphene cut electrical resistivity to one-110th of its original value. The total amount of conductive filler stayed the same.

My favourite example comes from DB Chem. It needed an antistatic plastic film, but even at 30% carbon black, the affordable grade couldn’t meet the target. With 15% carbon black and just 0.2% HydroGraph graphene, the film hit the target, was easier to form and cost about the same to formulate. That’s a result a purchasing manager can act on.

Then there’s Sparc Technologies. After 16 weeks of corrosion testing, rust had spread 25% less from a scratch in a commercial epoxy coating containing Sparc’s HydroGraph-based additive. Sparc says a successful 4,200-hour test would take the companies into negotiations for a supply agreement. That’s one potential customer with a specific result and a clear next decision.

CEO Kjirstin Breure’s two November interviews with Jay Taylor are worth putting together. On November 5, she explained how the graphene paste makes it easier for manufacturers to use the material. More than 30 customers have already received samples. In the November 19 follow-up, she discussed patents for specific applications, including conductive plastics, and said a manufacturer was already lined up to build more Hyperion reactors.

Several customers have moved on to negotiating prices, volumes and supply terms. And look at who HydroGraph hired this week to close those deals. New chief commercial officer Hector Miravete previously led commercial strategy for a Johnson Matthey catalyst portfolio generating more than $700 million in annual revenue. He knows what it takes to sell a specialized material to industrial buyers year after year.

Now put the capital requirements alongside the mining economics above. HydroGraph raised C$70.4 million. What does it cost to get Bellville up and running? Roughly US$8 million for the building and its first six reactors, according to CEO Kjirstin Breure. That gives HydroGraph about 60 tons of annual capacity at Bellville, with room to scale to 360 as orders come in.

I expect hockey-stick revenue growth to begin in 2027, and I see a credible path to break-even that year without another equity raise. The milestone I’m watching most closely is the first repeat order with meaningful volume. That’s when we start to learn what one qualified application is worth to HydroGraph every year. Then run the same exercise across plastics, coatings, cement and rubber. That’s why $HGRAF is my number one investment.

Just my weekend thoughts. As always, do your own DD.

I expect HydroGraph’s graphene sales to ramp up quickly once the company starts delivering on its first major contracts. Over time, I can see annual sales reaching tens of thousands of tonnes, possibly even hundreds of thousands. For 2027, I expect the ramp-up to begin. Those volumes are further down the road.

David Friedberg: Why the AI Job Loss Narrative is Bullsh*t

“The job loss narrative is bullsh*t. It's also why ‘Everyone is going to end up on welfare,’ is bullsh*t. (And) ‘We need the government to step in and provide UBI,’ is bullsh*t.

Because with any other kind of frontier moment in human history, it's the new jobs, the new industries get created before the old ones are irrelevant.

I think the biggest opportunity for AI is on the frontier. That is where basically businesses and people can do things that humans and businesses have never been able to do before.

And that means crafting solutions to really difficult engineering problems, to really difficult scientific problems, to previously intractable problems.

And that's where I think that the frontier gets expanded by 100x or 1,000x versus AI being some iteration on existing business processes to save money and make things more efficient, which is where people natively go because most people don't work on the frontier, and they're not pushing the envelope on what's possible.

So their mind is always about, ‘Well, how does this change my job?’ And then you immediately get fearful about your job getting recast.

And the truth is, that's not the typical use case. The typical use case where we spend time and spend tokens is doing things that we've never done before, figuring out how to solve those really tough problems, how to do it quickly, how to do it efficiently, and that means humans generally can expand our frontiers, our horizons.”

when I first met @bavaria_kush and @wayne_nelmz, they'd quit their jobs just a few weeks earlier. we spent the next few days trading notes and contract ideas over Signal, then met irl to whiteboard how these markets might work. shortly after, we signed a term sheet.

what struck me most was how curious, open-minded, and thoughtful they were.

markets are information dense and constantly evolving. building them requires intellectual openness alongside precision and discipline in execution, a rare balance for a founder to strike. 

i've watched Kush and Wayne leave money on the table to get deals done that make everyone better off. they understand that building a market means creating value for the entire ecosystem, not just capturing it for yourself.

He is going to hate me for saying this, but I think one of the smartest people in venture is @milesgrimshaw, hands down. 

So when he calls me and tells me about an incredible entrepreneur that I have to have on 20VC, I listen. 

He told me the tale of @bavaria_kush: 

- 23-year-old whiz 
- Built viral sports betting platform from his dorm at MIT 
- Started @OrnnExchange, the financial market for AI compute.
- Insanely profitable 

So I got on a call with him. Within 5 mins of the call, I asked him to join me on the show. 

I summarized the notes from our discussion below:

Thanks to @AdamValkin, @fachlib, @Melt_Dem for amazing questions. (Links in Comments)

--

1. Why NYC Is a Better Place to Build a Company Than SF

Kush argues that people in the Valley are coin-operated, so $100K more in pay or 50 bps more equity is enough to move a researcher to another company. New York has a culture of loyalty to colleagues and family, with much more camaraderie between people than in SF.

Love your thoughts on this given your time both in and outside the valley @paulg @rabois 

2. Humans Will Simply Be a Vessel to Carry AI Around the World

Kush believes AI will become so much smarter than people that humans end up as a biological vessel for it. The human role then is less about controlling AI and more about teaching it feelings and emotions, almost as a parent.

Love your thoughts on this @bryan_johnson and how that impacts your work?

3. How Undersupplied on Chips Are We Truly?

Compute is very undersupplied. Buying from CoreWeave today likely means a quote for Q4 2027 or Q1 2028. Building your own takes about half a year, with 20 to 22 weeks to get chips from OEMs, who tend to promise earlier dates, plus two to three weeks to install.

What does no one know that everyone should know about the current state of chip supply @andrewdfeldman @goodwin_ml @UbertiGavin 

4. Why Factory Is So Much Better Than Cognition

Ornn used Devin for a while, but the problem with Cognition was how expensive it was. Kush sees the two as competitors on the same product and says Factory is much cheaper to use. He also rates Factory's underlying harness above Devin's.

I am sure @shaunmmaguire will be smiling here. 

5. Why You Should Always Choose Boutique Investors Over Mega Fund Investors

Boutique investors care more about founders because their success is tied directly to the company's. Partners at boutique firms are often there for the mission, and the firm itself is like a startup trying to make its name, so they work extremely hard to make their companies succeed.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @wquist @honam @annbordetsky 

6. Why Infrastructure Investors Will Never Lose

Kush compares data centers to apartment buildings, with infrastructure investors as landlords and inference providers, OpenAI and Anthropic as tenants renting GPUs. As long as there are tenants, the landlords keep collecting rent. If enterprise demand weakens, GPU prices fall the way rents do in a bad economy.

7. Chip Prices in Three Years Could Be Higher Than Today

When Ornn started, many assumed GPU hour prices three to five years out would be lower, so contracts often included free options to renew at prices like $2.50. 

No one gives that for free now, because the market expects prices in three years may be higher than today. Kush would not be surprised to see $20 to $30 per GPU hour.

What does no one see that everyone should see about the price of compute moving forward @AnjneyMidha?

Taiwan regulators had announced these market control measures for their local stocks which become effective tomorrow (Nov 23):

> blanket ban on margin/covered shorts at below previous trading day's close

> min margin requirement for short sales raised from 130% to 150%

> temporary suspension of acceptance of new applications from securities houses to list new put warrants 

Short hedges are exempt from the ban (e.g. swaps underlying leveraged ETFs)

IMO, these measures had demonstrated to be ineffective, especially if markets are driven by macro and fundamental forces

They distort free market mechanisms, drive down liquidity and introduce bid-ask friction which makes hedging even more difficult

What they, and other market regulators, should do is educate the general public on the flows breakdown: program vs non-program trading, institutional vs retail, local vs foreign, etc so market participants can make well-informed trading and investment decisions on their own assessment of the market situation

We might lose the ability to tell how fast AI is improving precisely when it starts making its biggest discoveries. From now on it’s likely that the frontier is beyond human cognition. 

Navier–Stokes took roughly 100 hours, including formal verification. Now there’s a claimed proof of the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude. We’re burning through the problems humans spent generations identifying as hard.

What happens when those stop being the benchmark? An AI spends 400 hours discovering and solving something we need ten years to understand. We can check the proof, but can we appreciate the leap? Or do we just say “wow, that must have been difficult” and wait for it to explain?

Human understanding could become the bottleneck in measuring AI progress. The curve keeps climbing, but we’re increasingly late to see it…

You can learn a lot about the next AI breakthrough by just reading AI labs and RL env startups’ job posts.

I’ve been looking at OpenAI, Anthropic, Mercor etc… and cross-referencing what they’re hiring for with benchmarks models still struggle on. A few things stand out.

Anthropic has a computational chemistry role explicitly about building RL environments to teach Claude reaction prediction, synthesis planning, etc. They also want an antibody scientist to test AI-designed candidates and feed the experimental results back to researchers. Pretty concrete.

On OpenAI’s job board, the Science data role says their current focus is biology and chemistry. Both labs are also hiring people to build RL environments for chip design: generate hardware descriptions, verify them, optimize power and performance…

On Mercor, investment banking and private equity projects advertise $130–180/hour. They want experts to build financial tasks and review model outputs. Meanwhile, the leading full-task score on MBABench 2.0 is only 15.8%. Lots of room to improve there.

Same pattern in healthcare: Mercor recruits specialist physicians, OpenAI explicitly hires for health RL environments, and the published DAYJOB Healthcare evaluation tops out around 25%.

Obviously a job posting doesn’t guarantee a breakthrough. But when expert hiring, training environments and unsaturated benchmarks all point to the same work… that’s worth paying attention to.

My bets: healthcare, financial workflows, chemistry, computational biology and chip design.

In the September quarter, Qualcomm hit nearly $2B in quarterly auto revenue for the first time ($8B annual run rate), closing in on Infineon at $2.45B and NXP at $2.07B. Qualcomm has already overtaken traditional auto semi companies such as TI, STMicro, Renesas, Analog Devices and onsemi. (1/7)🧵

thread_tweets.text:
Back in Oct-2016, when Qualcomm tried to buy NXP for $47B, NXP’s auto business was 8.6x the size of Qualcomm’s. Last quarter that ratio was down to 1.04x.
Even without the NXP deal, Qualcomm went past Analog Devices in 2Q24, onsemi in 1Q25, Renesas in 4Q25, STMicro in 1Q26 and Texas Instruments in 3Q26 (by our estimate). (2/7)

Qualcomm has beaten every auto target it has set. It guided $1.5B for fiscal 2024 and did $2.9B, guided $3.5B for fiscal 2026 and did $6.0B, and exited the year at an $8.0B annual rate five years ahead of its old fiscal 2031 goal.
Qualcomm targets $10B in auto semi revenue by fiscal 2029. If Infineon grows about 10% a year after fiscal 2027 as its CEO expects, it will reach roughly $12.4B, so Qualcomm will need to beat its target by about 25% to hold #1. (4/7)

Qualcomm sidestepped traditional competitors like Infineon, NXP and TI in power chips, microcontrollers, analog and sensors. It went straight after digital cockpit, ADAS and connectivity, buying Arriver (2022) for ADAS software and Autotalks (2025) for V2X safety chips to offer a complete hardware-and-software platform.
That compute and connectivity business grew 89% from a year ago at Qualcomm last quarter, while Infineon and NXP grew 10% to 13%. (6/7)

Passing Infineon in 2027 comes down to quarterly math and FX. Infineon guided fiscal 2027 Automotive up mid-teens to roughly $10.3B at 1.15 EUR/USD (helped by moving onboard chargers into the segment), and both companies guided the December quarter flat.

At 12% quarterly growth next year (half its recent 20% to 25% pace), Qualcomm passes NXP in 1Q27, overtakes Infineon on quarterly revenue in 3Q27 ($2.80B vs $2.68B), and wins calendar 2027 ($10.7B vs $10.5B). Winning fiscal 2027 takes 17.5% quarterly growth after December. (7/7)
